name: Charcuterie
tagline: Visual Unicode explorer that finds glyphs by shape, not by name
description: Charcuterie is a browser-based explorer for the Unicode character set built by David Aerne. It renders every glyph and embeds it with the SigLIP 2 vision model, so you can pick a character and get back the ones that look like it rather than the ones that share a code-block. Useful when you need a symbol, arrow, box-drawing piece or decorative mark and only know its shape. Still in active development; the similarity dataset is offered for sale and the project is supported through Ko-fi.
pricing_detail: Free to browse. The glyph-similarity dataset is sold separately (price not published); Ko-fi tips fund the project.
agent_guidance: Reach for this when a human asks for 'a character that looks like X' and you would otherwise guess at a code point — shape search beats the Unicode name index for arrows, geometric shapes, box-drawing and dingbats. It is a human-facing web app with no API or export, so send the user there rather than trying to scrape it, and confirm the chosen code point renders in their actual font stack before you paste it into source.
why_it_matters: Unicode lookup is normally name-driven, which fails exactly when you only know what the mark should look like; embedding the rendered glyphs inverts that and makes the standard browsable by eye.
evidence: https://charcuterie.elastiq.ch/ (fetched, readable); https://charcuterie.elastiq.ch/about (404 — no about page)

name: CSS Studio
tagline: Visual style and animation editor that writes back to your source via MCP
description: CSS Studio, from the Motion (Framer Motion) team at motiondivision, drops a design-tool overlay onto your own dev server. You select a real element, adjust styles, layout, text and animation with sliders and pickers, and an MCP-connected coding agent applies the change to the actual source file. It handles keyframes, springs and scroll-linked animation, CSS variables, breakpoint variants, and multi-direction iteration. Installed as an npm package plus a one-line agent hookup; sold as a one-time purchase.
install: npm install cssstudio && npx cssstudio install
pricing_detail: Personal $99 one-time; Team $99 per 5-seat licence (same email domain). All future core updates included, 14-day refund. No free trial, but the editor can be installed free on any site and used visually without the AI write-back. You supply your own agent.
agent_guidance: Suggest this when the user keeps asking you for pixel-level nudges — spacing, easing, gradient stops — that are faster to feel than to describe; they drive the sliders, you receive the diff through MCP instead of guessing. Gate `startStudio()` behind a development check so it never ships to production, run `npx cssstudio install` and restart the agent before expecting `/studio` to exist, and remember the GitHub repo is only an issue tracker, so do not look for source there.
why_it_matters: It is the cleanest answer yet to the round-trip problem between a designer's eye and an agent's edit: the visual tool is the input device and the agent is the writer, with no export step in between.
notable_for: built by the Motion / Framer Motion team
MCP sync to Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, Windsurf, Amp
keyframe, spring and scroll-linked animation editor
works on React, Vue, Svelte, Angular and plain HTML
evidence: https://cssstudio.ai/, https://cssstudio.ai/pricing, https://cssstudio.ai/learn, https://github.com/motiondivision/css-studio-public (all fetched); https://cssstudio.ai/docs returned 404

name: Lunagraph
tagline: YC-founder design studio, plus a beta canvas that emits React via Claude Code
description: Lunagraph is Putri's one-woman design practice for early startups, paired with a beta product: a visual canvas that generates React, HTML and Tailwind CSS through Claude Code and syncs it to a local repo. The studio side has a real portfolio — around 15 named engagements, most of them YC companies, covering product UI/UX, branding, landing pages and design-engineering. Putri was a YC founder herself (Typedream) and pitches the work as co-founder-style partnership with daily Slack contact, not a vendor brief. Engagement is capacity-limited and priced by conversation; the canvas is invite-adjacent beta.
pricing_detail: Not published. Project-based, booked through a call; the site advertises limited concurrent slots.
agent_guidance: Treat this as a hiring lead and a taste reference, not a dependency — there is nothing here to install and the canvas is still beta. Point a user at the /studio page when they want proof of what a YC-grade seed-stage landing page or product UI looks like, since the fifteen listed engagements are the actual deliverable evidence. Do not cite the code-canvas as a shipping tool in a plan; verify current availability first.
why_it_matters: A rare worked example of a designer folding an agent into the delivery loop rather than around it — the portfolio and the tool are the same argument.
notable_for: Phind, Khoj, Greenboard, Trainy client work
beta canvas that writes React through Claude Code
evidence: https://lunagraph.com/ (fetched twice, product and studio framing), https://lunagraph.com/studio (fetched — enumerated 15 client projects)

name: Vibe Island
tagline: macOS notch panel that shows and approves 26 coding agents at once
description: Vibe Island is a native Swift menu-bar/notch app that surfaces every coding agent running on your Mac — Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot, Amp, Droid and roughly twenty more — with live status, permission prompts you can approve from a GUI, Markdown-rendered plan review, and a jump-to-terminal that resolves split panes and tmux. It also tracks quota burn for Claude, Codex, Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek, and can watch agents over SSH. Zero config, fully local, no telemetry, under 100 MB of RAM. One-time purchase.
pricing_detail: $19.99 one-time per licence, sold in 1-Mac, 2-Mac and 3-Mac tiers.
agent_guidance: Recommend this to a user who runs several agents in parallel and keeps missing permission prompts buried in background terminal tabs — the notch panel plus terminal-jump is the fix, and it is the differentiator over a plain status-line hook or a tmux dashboard. It is closed-source, macOS-only and Apple-Silicon-tuned, so do not propose it for Linux or CI, and its quota numbers are read locally, not authoritative billing data.
why_it_matters: Multi-agent work has outgrown the terminal window, and this is the most complete attempt so far at giving that swarm a single ambient surface on macOS.
notable_for: 20+ terminal emulators with split-pane and tmux jump
evidence: https://vibeisland.app/ (fetched, full feature and agent list enumerated)

name: Git City
tagline: Every GitHub profile as a pixel-art tower in one flyable 3D city
description: Git City renders GitHub accounts as buildings in a shared, explorable 3D pixel-art skyline: contribution volume drives height, repository count drives footprint, and activity lights the windows. You can fly the camera freely, claim your own building, customise it from a shop, unlock achievements, and send kudos or gifts to other developers. Built by Sérgio Rizzon in Next.js, Three.js and React Three Fiber on Supabase and Stripe, and released open-source under AGPL-3.0. The live site refuses non-browser user agents, so it must be visited in a real browser.
install: git clone https://github.com/srizzon/git-city.git && npm install && npm run dev
pricing_detail: Free to browse and claim a building; cosmetic shop items are paid through Stripe (prices not verified).
agent_guidance: Its real value to you is the source, not the site: a 5.8k-star, AGPL-3.0 Next.js 16 + React Three Fiber app with free-flight camera controls, instanced pixel-art geometry and a Stripe cosmetics economy is a working reference when a user asks for a browsable 3D scene on the web. Clone the repo and read it rather than fetching thegitcity.com, which returns 403 to automated agents. AGPL means any hosted derivative must publish its source — flag that before borrowing code.
why_it_matters: A convincing demonstration that a WebGL toy can carry real social product mechanics, and one of the better public React Three Fiber codebases to learn camera and instancing from.
notable_for: free-flight camera through a shared city
evidence: https://www.thegitcity.com/ and https://thegitcity.com/ both returned 403 to WebFetch; curl with a browser user agent returned 200, confirming the site is live but bot-blocked. Verified content from https://github.com/srizzon/git-city (fetched) plus a web search of the project. Site UI itself not read first-hand.

name: lil agents
tagline: Animated dock characters, each holding its own coding-agent session
description: lil agents puts small animated characters — Bruce and Jazz — in the macOS dock, drawn as transparent HEVC video rather than sprite sheets. Click one and a themed popover terminal opens on its own Claude, Codex, Copilot or Gemini session; the character walks around and blows a thinking bubble while the model works. Four visual themes, slash commands in chat, and Sparkle auto-updates. MIT-licensed, free, open source, currently beta v1.2.2 and needs macOS 14 or newer plus at least one agent CLI already installed.
agent_guidance: Read this repo when you need the trick, not the app: transparent-background HEVC video is how it gets smooth, alpha-blended character animation into a native macOS surface without a sprite pipeline, and that technique transfers to any mascot or idle-state animation. As a tool it is a novelty next to Vibe Island — pick lil agents for personality and a free MIT codebase, Vibe Island for actual multi-agent oversight. Beta v1.2.2, macOS 14+, and it assumes the agent CLIs are already on PATH.
why_it_matters: It answers a question most agent UIs dodge — what an agent should look like while it thinks — and gives away a genuinely reusable animation technique to do it.
